s10.slug: SUNDAY · 9:05 PM · N. DUPRE STREET — THE STREET
s10.music: Dirty Dozen Brass Band — “My Feet Can’t Fail Me Now”
body: The first thing is the noise. It comes out of every door on Dupre Street at once, out of the screen doors and the open windows and down the steep steps, and it brings the people with it: men in jerseys with their arms over their heads, women with pot lids and soup spoons, a little boy on his father’s shoulders hitting a cowbell with a wrench, a grandmother in a quilted housecoat beating a saucepan with a meat tenderizer, down into the road under every porch light on the block. A nun in a gold sweatshirt goes by on a bicycle, ringing the bell on her handlebars the length of the street. Two doors down a man has a trumpet he can’t play, and he is playing it, the first three notes of something, over and over. Out on Esplanade the car horns have started, every horn on the avenue leaning on the Who Dat. A fire truck crosses the end of the street with its lights turning and its siren going, and the men riding the back step have their helmets off and are waving them.

Over the roofs somebody sets off fireworks that, from the size of them, he has been saving since 1967. They go up green and gold over the oaks and come apart, and the smoke drifts down into the street and hangs under the branches in the porch light, powder and cigars and somebody’s grill and, under all that, something sweet off a tree in a yard he can’t see.

Halfway down the block a pickup is parked with both doors open and the radio turned up as far as it goes, a tuba walking along the bottom of a song and the horns piling in on top of it, and in front of its headlights people who were strangers at the kickoff are dancing in the road.

The Broussards are all through it. A woman in a flannel nightgown and a Brees jersey comes down off her porch in her slippers, takes Nonc Clovis’s face in both hands and kisses him on the mouth, lets go of him, and goes on up the street to find somebody else, and Clovis stands in the road with his visor in his hand. Aints III sits down on the center line, puts his head back and howls, and three houses’ worth of dogs answer him. Remy is standing on the roof of a parked Camry with both arms up, and the Camry’s owner is standing on its hood below him with both arms up, and the Camry is holding. Up on the porch somebody has put Mémère in the swing with a blanket over her knees and her beads in her lap, and people come up the steep steps one after another to kiss her, and to each of them she says *merci*. Celeste sits on the top step below her with Lucille against her shoulder, laughing and crying into the black-and-gold cap, and Lucille is awake and furious about all of it.

Tony is off the porch. He got as far as the curb. He is bent over the hood of a stranger’s car, a green Grand Am with a Mississippi plate, with his arms spread across it and his face down on the metal and his sport coat rucked up over the Brees jersey, crying with his shoulders, and the man who owns the Grand Am, in a Shockey jersey, stands over him patting him on the back in a slow, steady rhythm, and is crying too.

Jack is in the middle of the street. The Broussards’ front room came out the door behind him and went in every direction, Kevin steering Margot by the elbow, Theo carrying Laney down the steps because she had lost a shoe, the twins over the rail. A man he has never seen in his life has hugged him twice. A girl in gold face paint has kissed him on the ear on her way past, and somebody put a can of Abita in his hand, and somebody else took it. Up and down Dupre Street people are holding on to each other in the road under the porch lights: cousins, neighbors, strangers, a couple in matching gold wigs, two old men who got up out of their lawn chairs at the same time and haven’t let go yet, the dancers in front of the truck. He has turned around, toward the house.
She comes off the curb at a run.
She is in her socks on the asphalt, her hair coming down out of the pencil, the medal swinging out on its chain, and she’s in his arms before either of them thinks.

He has her up off the road and down again. Her arms are round his neck. His are round her back, and the city goes off around them, the pot lids, the horns, the fire truck coming back round the block the other way, a whistle somewhere, the trumpet. She is shaking. Her ribs go in and out against his, fast, and the back of her shirt is damp under his hands, and her ear is cold against his cheek and the rest of her is hot. Her socks are soaked from the road. Somewhere in it she has stepped up onto his shoes to get out of the wet, and she stands there.
She leans back far enough to see his face. She keeps her hands on his arms to do it.
The light off her mother’s porch is on her. Her face is wet to the chin. She’s laughing up at him with the hair across one eye, a laugh he can hear over the trumpet, and then the laugh stops.

Her face stays turned up to his. Her lips are parted, and nothing comes out of them. And there is something in it Jack can read, the way he reads the sky over the South Side in December, the hour before snow: low and close and yellow-gray, the streetlights on at four in the afternoon, the air gone still, and nothing falling yet.

There is gold paint on her cheekbone, a fleur-de-lis some stranger thumbed onto her between the porch and the curb, half of it gone now into the front of his shirt. Over her shoulder the Camry’s owner has climbed down off his hood to kiss his wife on the sidewalk, and two strangers in Saints wigs are kissing against a lamppost, and the woman in the nightgown has found somebody else.

Behind her a man is beating a saucepan with a spoon. The trumpet two doors down finds a fourth note at last, and loses it. His hands are open on her back, and they stay open. Her hands stay on his arms.

choices.key: In the street after the game, with the whole city going off, Lena came off the curb into your arms. You said her name, and nothing after it.
response: Her name, and nothing after it. She puts her hand up to his face, cold from the street, and holds it there, and doesn’t answer it.

choices.key: In the street after the game, with the whole city going off, Lena came off the curb into your arms. You didn’t say anything. You held on.
response: He says nothing. He holds on, and she lets him, and the dancers from in front of the truck come down the road in a line with their handkerchiefs going and split around the two of them and close up again on the other side.

choices.key: In the street after the game, with the whole city going off, Lena came off the curb into your arms. You said: Who dat. She said it back, into your collar.
response: She laughs, wet, with her face gone into his neck, and says it back into his collar: “Who *dat*.”

s10a.slug: SUNDAY · 9:15 PM · N. DUPRE STREET — THE HOOD OF A BUICK

body.text: Her hand is still on his face when Tony gets there.

body: He comes across the road from the Grand Am with his face wet and his sport coat open and the Brees jersey dark at the collar, and he doesn’t slow down for either of them. He takes Jack round the middle in both arms and lifts him clean off Dupre Street, so that Jack’s shoes hang over the asphalt. He smells of rye and bitters and somebody else’s cigar. Into Jack’s ear, with what four quarters of radio have left of his voice, he says it:

He sets Jack down and takes him by the back of the neck and shakes him, the way you’d shake a radio to bring the station back, and lets go to grab somebody else. Josie has Lena by the wrist. She tows her backward across the road to the steps, where Tess is reaching for her, and Clovis, and the family closes over her in the porch light.

Jack steps back out of the road to the far curb, where a maroon Buick LeSabre is parked across from the Broussards’ steps with a Saints flag in its back window. He brings both hands down on its hood. The hood booms. He puts his head back and roars at the sky over Dupre Street, at the smoke and the oaks and the dark over the roofs with no stars in it, roars till there is nothing left in his chest to do it with.

Dupre Street roars back. Every porch on the block is doing it, men pounding the hoods of cars and the posts of porches and each other, women with their heads back and their eyes shut, a city with its mouth open at the sky, and his is one more. He brings his hands down on the hood again, harder, and the Buick’s alarm goes off, whooping, and the street cheers the alarm.

When he straightens up off the hood, Theo and Laney are at the bottom of the Broussards’ steps across the road. Laney has Theo by both lapels of his good coat and is shaking him, hard, and Theo is letting her; his head goes back and forth with it, and the iPhone in his hand is filming the sidewalk. Her mouth is going a mile a minute. Their eyes aren’t on any screen in any window. They go to the Buick, and to the steps, and back to the Buick, and Laney shakes him harder.

Kevin is out in the middle of the road with his BlackBerry to one ear and a finger in the other, dialing. The network gives him nothing, and nothing again, and on the ninth or tenth try it gives him something. “Clare,” he says. “Clare. It’s Kevin. From Louisiana.” A small voice in the BlackBerry says something back. He holds the phone up over his head, out to the pot lids and the horns and the Buick, and brings it back down. “Can you hear it? Clare, that’s — that’s *all of it*.” He turns in the road with the phone at his ear, and his eyes come round to Jack at the Buick, and go on across the street to Lena on her mother’s steps, and come back.
“Hold on,” Kevin says into the phone. “Everyone’s healthy.”
Margot, kissed on the cheek in passing by a stranger in a Brees jersey, stands in the road with her notebook in her coat pocket and doesn’t take it out.
From the Broussards’ steps Remy finds Jack across the road and throws both arms up. “*Brother-in-law!*” The crowd in front of the truck takes him, and he goes into it dancing.
Nonc Clovis goes past with the nightgown woman’s lipstick on his mouth and Aints III under one arm like a sack of feed, looking up the block the way she went.

Jude comes along the curb with a pot lid under his arm. He is thirteen, in a Saints jersey that reaches his knees, and so far he has communicated with Jack entirely by eating things in front of him. He stops. He looks up.
“Who dat,” Jude says, and goes on down the curb, hitting the pot lid with his fist.

Celeste comes across the road last, without the baby. She stops beside him at the Buick, with its alarm going, and puts her hand on his arm. All day she has been putting things into his hands: the Igloo, the ice, a plate for Tony. Her hands are empty now.
“Bring them home, baby,” she says, in her whisper, and under the alarm it reaches him anyway.
She isn’t looking at him when she says it. She is looking across the street, at the steps, at Lena.

In his jeans the RAZR has found nothing since the two-minute warning. Every phone in the city is trying at once, and the network has given up and gone out into the street with everybody else. It buzzes against his hip anyway.

body.text: tell the saints girls father congratulations

body: Pop.

Jack takes it across the road. Tony is back at the Grand Am with the man in the Shockey jersey, the two of them leaning on it like a bar. Jack holds the phone out. Tony takes it in his big hand and holds it at arm’s length under the streetlight, and reads it with his lips moving, and lays it face-up on the hood of the stranger’s car, carefully, like a full glass. He climbs up on the Grand Am’s bumper, and the man in the Shockey jersey steadies him by the belt.
“His *daddy*,” Tony tells Dupre Street, with an arm flung out at Jack. “In *Ohio*.”

And Dupre Street, which has never heard of Frank Costigan, cheers him: the porches, the truck, the dancers in its headlights, the woman in the nightgown from halfway up the block. The man in the Shockey jersey hands Jack back his phone and shakes his hand, and somebody else shakes it, and somebody else, and his palms are still stinging from the Buick’s hood, both of them, to the wrist.

journal.title: Celeste Broussard
journal.text: Lena’s mother. A nurse — she came to the door in scrubs. Gives her orders in a whisper. Saturday night she was in the door when I came up her steps with Lena asleep, and she didn’t ask me one thing. Sunday she ran eleven people through one bathroom in a whisper. Ice, baby. In the street after the game, with the whole city yelling, she said to me: Bring them home, baby.

journal.title: Tony Broussard
journal.text: Lena’s father. Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Twenty-eight years in the same seats. Held the phone up to the kitchen radio for the whole second half while we lost him at every curve on Highway 1. Wes told him there’s a Browns fan out here. Laney had him at hello. Saturday night in the side yard he put me on the paddle inside ten minutes. Sunday in the pew he told God He owes him one. He wouldn’t watch the game; he listened on the porch, on the radio, with his eyes shut. When it was over he cried face-down on the hood of a stranger’s car, and then he picked me up off the street.

journal.title: Kevin Tran
journal.text: Kevin Tran. Goes to daily Mass, saves you a seat with a Bible. Has a sister, Tina, in dental school, who flossed in the womb. Lies to his mom about orgo in Vietnamese. Drives his mother’s Odyssey at sixty-five, not sixty-six. His dad has two nail-salon supply stores in San Jose and has never had a Labor Day. Brought six pairs of gloves to a beach cleanup. Mouthed every word of Joey’s first reading from the second pew. Somebody coached Joey; I can guess who. Brought tea to a wake. His Bà Nội says heaven makes the elephant and heaven makes the grass. Walked Margot down at four in the morning. Handed Lena a roll of quarters for the payphone before she asked. Halloween: All Saints, every one nobody’s heard of — scrubs, a halo and a white mask. He found Laney. Friday night a pre-med said Maine got it right. Kevin answered him and went to get water. Tuesday, the Vietnamese Martyrs: his mother reads eleven of the hundred and seventeen. Asked about the scar. Alarm Five, on the lawn: he had a question mark next to my name on his clipboard. I told Priya I was out. He erased it. Tuesday at four I woke him for Doug. A chair under the knob, then a bell. Wednesday at the Brick, at the next carrel all night: ‘You two have been defending each other for three hours. That isn’t studying.’ Sings bass. A real one. Seven years of Vietnamese choir in San Jose — his mother made him. Friday, from the Odyssey: Go home. Sleep. Tell somebody something. Back from San Jose. His mother has a girl from their parish she wants him to call. Clare. She plays the violin in the Mass band. Wednesday he brought two flats of water to the Haiti table, which nobody asked for, and stayed to hold Clare’s violin case. ‘My mother knows your mother.’ Thursday he called Clare. His mother had the number, and his grandmother was on the speaker. She said yes to Sully’s. MLK Day he brought gloves for everybody. Tuesday in the basement he read us the first reading off his BlackBerry. Clare’s going to the Walk for Life, and so is he. He asked me to come — for him. I said yes. Thursday at the window table he had a list: things to say at hour four. He’d heard about Hale’s — Laney to Margot to him — and didn’t take a side. Then he asked me what you’re supposed to feel at hour four. I told him. He wrote it down. Clare asked him which of us was right at Hale’s; he told her he didn’t have the information, and she said that was a very Kevin answer. He asked if my brother’s okay. Thursday night at the van he had a clipboard and a seating chart taped to the dash, and said he’s pre-med, not a switchboard. Clare came to see him off. At three in the morning he was at St. Brendan’s ahead of me. Couldn’t sleep either. At a quarter to five Osei blessed his mother’s car again. Still pretty blessed. Friday under the dinosaurs at Cabazon he told Theo and Laney to leave it alone. He checked the oil at the Arizona line. He called Clare from El Paso, like he said he would. He kept the clock the whole way: thirty-five hours and forty minutes. Sunday night in the street he called Clare from Louisiana, like he said he would, and held the phone up so she could hear it. Everyone’s healthy, he told her.

journal.title: Dad
journal.text: Frank Costigan. Twenty-six years on the line at Lordstown, laid off since June. Drove me 2,400 miles because two plane tickets cost more than the truck is worth. Saw the Pacific for the first time today. Didn’t say anything. That’s how you know. Monday the 9th: the SUB pay’s done. He went to the bar for the Steelers and didn’t come home. Sat in the employee lot at Lordstown to see if the lights were on. Hit the trash can pulling in at ten to five. Ma called me at one. Nobody was hurt. Saturday he called about Ohio State. Overtime. Pasadena. First time since September. Thanksgiving: sober. Washed the truck. Picked us up at Pittsburgh and talked to Theo the whole way home. Guest says grace — his rule. Told Theo to come back. You don’t call first. Friday morning, a voicemail: Browns beat Pittsburgh. Thirteen–six. Eight sacks. Thought I’d want to know. Christmas: waited at the bottom of the escalator in Pittsburgh with a thermos and asked about the girl, because Ma told him to. Ginger ale at the bar, in a glass. Stayed in the truck at Trumbull — the twenty-seventh, he says. Drove Theo and me up Christmas Eve and stayed in the truck again. Told Theo Danny ate everything at eleven. Two-eighty-six. Gave Theo the parka without a word. “You’re not company.” Held the 1964 program a long time. On Skye: “Huh.” Asked me what it’s like in there. Went in on Holy Family Sunday — his name was on the list at the desk; he asked Ma where he’s supposed to stand. Told Danny about the hall and the Cruze, and laughed, in there. Asked if the Saints girl sent the coffee. I said yeah. Told Danny they wouldn’t lose. Three straight. His phone died in the cold and he borrowed mine. New Year’s: a ginger ale, in a glass. New Year’s: two spoons of lentils, for the money. “Pryor.” Went in to see Danny again. “Four straight.” Twelfth Night we took the lights down, and the beer fridge is ginger ale now. At the curb in Pittsburgh: call your mother when you land. She don’t sleep. Thursday he called me — him, not Ma. He put sixty dollars in my account for gas. It ain’t a question. Theo e-mailed Ma a budget, with a chart. Watch it with people, he says; that’s the whole thing. Tell the TV one Ma says Canada’s cold. Sunday night after the game his text got through when nothing else would: tell the saints girls father congratulations. I showed Tony. Tony read it out to the street.
